OK.label: No change
OK.headline: No change needed
OK.explanation: You do not need to change this medicine because of your kidneys.

DOSE.label: Dose check
DOSE.headline: Dose may need adjusting – check with your clinician
DOSE.explanation: Weaker kidneys clear this medicine more slowly. Your doctor or pharmacist may need to lower the dose or space it out.

ASK.label: Consult doctor
ASK.headline: Consult your doctor
ASK.explanation: This may be OK only in some cases. Ask your doctor before you take it.

AVOID.label: Not recommended
AVOID.headline: Not recommended
AVOID.explanation: It is best not to take this medicine at your kidney level.

NA.label: Can't assess
NA.headline: This cannot be assessed
NA.explanation: We don't have enough information to give guidance. Ask your doctor or pharmacist.

EGFR.label: Needs eGFR
EGFR.headline: (depends on eGFR – see eGFR follow-up column)
EGFR.explanation: The app asks for the eGFR number; see the eGFR follow-up column.

safety_message: Because your doctor prescribed this, do not stop or change it on your own. Call your doctor's office to make sure they know your kidney stage.
transplant_message: This cannot be assessed – ask your transplant team

M01.name: Ibuprofen
M01.note: Ibuprofen is an NSAID. It is a type of pain medicine that can hurt the kidneys. Do not use it if you are sick, throwing up, or not drinking enough. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is often a safer choice. Ask your doctor.

M02.name: Ibuprofen (prescribed)
M02.note: Ibuprofen is an NSAID. Your doctor should use the lowest dose for the shortest time and may check your kidney blood tests.

M03.name: Naproxen
M03.note: Naproxen is an NSAID. It is a type of pain medicine that can hurt the kidneys. Do not use it if you are sick, throwing up, or not drinking enough. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is often a safer choice. Ask your doctor.

M04.name: Naproxen (prescribed)
M04.note: Naproxen is an NSAID. Your doctor should use the lowest dose for the shortest time and may check your kidney blood tests.

M05.name: Meloxicam
M05.note: Meloxicam is an NSAID, a type of pain medicine that can hurt the kidneys. Your doctor may check your kidney blood tests.

M06.name: Diclofenac (pills)
M06.note: Diclofenac is an NSAID, a type of pain medicine that can hurt the kidneys. Your doctor may check your kidney blood tests.

M07.name: Diclofenac gel
M07.note: Diclofenac gel is an NSAID rubbed on the skin. Less reaches the blood than with pills, but ask your doctor first if you have kidney disease.

M08.name: Celecoxib
M08.note: Celecoxib is an NSAID-type pain medicine that can hurt the kidneys. Your doctor may check your kidney blood tests.

M09.name: Aspirin – high dose (325 mg or more)
M09.note: Aspirin at pain doses (325 mg or more) acts like an NSAID. It can hurt the kidneys and cause bleeding.

M10.name: Aspirin – low dose (81 mg), self-started
M10.note: Low-dose aspirin (81 mg) is usually safe for the kidneys. It can raise the risk of bleeding, so tell your doctor you take it.

M11.name: Aspirin – low dose (81 mg), doctor recommended
M11.note: Keep taking it the way your doctor told you.

M12.name: Acetaminophen
M12.note: Usually the safest pain medicine for the kidneys. Do not take more than 3,000 mg a day unless your doctor says so. Many cold and sleep products also have acetaminophen in them. Count those too.

M13.name: Magnesium hydroxide
M13.note: Weak kidneys can't get rid of extra magnesium well. Too much magnesium can make you weak and cause heart rhythm problems.

M14.name: Magnesium citrate
M14.note: Weak kidneys can't get rid of extra magnesium well. Too much magnesium can make you weak and cause heart rhythm problems.

M15.name: Aluminum / magnesium antacid
M15.note: These antacids have magnesium and aluminum in them. Both can build up when the kidneys are weak.

M16.name: Sodium phosphate enema or bowel prep
M16.note: Phosphate products can cause sudden kidney damage. Ask your doctor about a choice that has no phosphate.

M17.name: Pseudoephedrine
M17.note: Usually fine with mild kidney disease. If your kidneys work less well, high doses taken for a long time can cause confusion. Some Sudafed products (Sudafed PE) have phenylephrine, which can raise blood pressure. Ask your doctor first if you have high blood pressure.

M18.name: Vitamin C supplements
M18.note: A daily multivitamin is usually fine. If your kidneys are weak, ask your doctor before you take extra vitamin C. High doses can build up.

notes_by_result.ASK: High dose may be unsafe. Ask your doctor for dose guidance.

M19.name: Vitamin D supplements (not prescribed)
M19.note: A daily multivitamin is usually fine. If your kidneys are weak, ask your doctor before you take extra vitamin D. High doses can build up.

notes_by_result.ASK: High dose may be unsafe. Ask your doctor for dose guidance.

M20.name: Vitamin D – prescribed
M20.note: Take it the way your doctor prescribed.

M21.name: Vitamin A supplements
M21.note: A daily multivitamin is usually fine. If your kidneys are weak, ask your doctor before you take extra vitamin A. High doses can build up.

notes_by_result.ASK: High dose may be unsafe. Ask your doctor for dose guidance.

M22.name: Gabapentin
M22.note: Weak kidneys clear gabapentin slowly. A normal dose can build up and cause sleepiness, dizziness, or falls.

M23.name: Pregabalin
M23.note: Weak kidneys clear pregabalin slowly. A normal dose can build up and cause sleepiness, dizziness, or falls.

M24.name: Oxycodone
M24.note: Oxycodone can build up when the kidneys are weak. This can cause too much sleepiness or slow breathing.

M25.name: Tramadol
M25.note: Tramadol can build up when the kidneys are weak. This raises the risk of seizures and sleepiness.

M26.name: Meperidine
M26.note: When the kidneys are weak, a breakdown product of meperidine builds up. It can cause seizures.

M27.name: Codeine
M27.note: When the kidneys are weak, codeine breakdown products build up. They can cause too much sleepiness.

M28.name: Morphine
M28.note: When the kidneys are weak, morphine breakdown products build up. They can cause too much sleepiness or slow breathing.

M29.name: Baclofen
M29.note: Baclofen builds up when the kidneys are weak. It can cause confusion or heavy sleepiness.

M30.name: Duloxetine
M30.note: Duloxetine builds up when the kidneys are very weak.

M31.name: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
M31.note: Your dose may need to be lower. This antibiotic can also raise potassium, so your doctor may check your blood work.

M32.name: Ciprofloxacin
M32.note: Weak kidneys clear this antibiotic more slowly. The dose may need to be lower.

M33.name: Levofloxacin
M33.note: Weak kidneys clear this antibiotic more slowly. The dose may need to be lower.

M34.name: Nitrofurantoin
M34.note: This antibiotic treats urine infections. When the kidneys are weak, it may not work well and can cause side effects.

M35.name: Valacyclovir
M35.note: Too much valacyclovir can cause confusion in people with weak kidneys. The dose may need to be lower.

M36.name: Metformin
M36.note: If your kidneys work less well, metformin should not be started. People who already take it may need a lower dose. Below eGFR 30, it should not be used.

M37.name: Glyburide
M37.note: Glyburide can build up when the kidneys are weak. This can make your blood sugar drop too low, which can be dangerous.

M38.name: SGLT2 inhibitors
M38.note: These medicines protect the kidneys and heart for many people. With very low kidney function, ask your doctor whether you should keep taking it. They are not used on dialysis.

M39.name: Emtricitabine / tenofovir DF
M39.note: Tenofovir can harm the kidneys. Whether it is OK depends on why you take it (HIV treatment or PrEP), so ask your doctor.

M40.name: Allopurinol
M40.note: If your kidneys are weak, you will most likely start allopurinol at a low dose.

M41.name: Colchicine
M41.note: Colchicine can build up when the kidneys are weak. Some other medicines also make it build up. Tell your pharmacist about everything you take.

M42.name: Lithium
M42.note: Lithium can harm the kidneys over time and builds up when they are weak. You need regular blood tests.

M43.name: Phenylephrine
M43.note: Phenylephrine is a decongestant that can raise blood pressure. Ask your doctor first if you have high blood pressure. With lower kidney function, ask your doctor before taking it.

M44.name: Metformin (not prescribed)
M44.note: Do not start metformin at this kidney stage unless your doctor says so.

M45.name: Acyclovir
M45.note: Too much acyclovir can cause confusion in people with weak kidneys. The dose may need to be lower.

M46.name: Emtricitabine / tenofovir alafenamide (TAF)
M46.note: Descovy (TAF) is the newer form of tenofovir. It is easier on the kidneys than the older form (Truvada, also called TDF).
